title: Redwood POC weekly sync - benchmark results vs baseline provider
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark numbers (latency & throughput) vs baseline provider. Redwood SE walked through latest run results, discussed batching and KV cache impacts, and proposed tuning steps for next run. Customer flagged on-prem network constraints and SLO targets; agreed on follow-ups including on-prem perf run, updated benchmark spreadsheet, and SOC2 docs share.
topics: benchmark numbers (p99 latency, avg latency, tokens/sec)
on-prem network constraints and VPC testing

Maya Singh - Run on-prem perf test with 8k seq and 2x batching, share logs - 2026-04-12

Sophie Liu - Share VPC peering/network config and throughput limits - 2026-04-09

Customer to validate network throughput for on-prem test and send config

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-05
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~42m
Attendees: John Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Emily Chen (Astra CTO), Raj Patel (Astra ML Eng), Sophie Liu (Astra Infra), Tom Harris (Astra PM)

[00:00] John Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly sync, appreciate you making time. Quick agenda, Maya will walk through the benchmark results we ran Thursday vs the baseline provider, then we'll talk tuning and next steps. Sound good?

[00:18] Emily Chen: Yep sounds good, thanks John.

[00:20] Maya Singh: Cool, I'll share my screen. So this is the run we did on Thu night, summary first: workload is our standard AstraHealth summarization workload — mix of 1k and 4k sequences with a 2-1 read/write ratio. Baseline provider (CloudVendorX) numbers are in column A, Redwood dedicated numbers in column B.

[00:45] Maya Singh: Key highlights: p99 latency on baseline was about 1.8s per request for 1k seq, Redwood p99 was 1.2s — so about 33% improvement. For 4k seq, baseline p99 was 3.9s, Redwood p99 2.7s. Throughput (tokens/sec) increased from ~420 tok/s to ~610 tok/s on same GPU type with our batching and kernel selection.

[01:15] Raj Patel: Sorry can you repeat the GPU type? Was that the same instance shape?

[01:19] Maya Singh: Yes same instance family — we ran both on g-proc-16x (equivalent), same quantization at q4x. We tuned kernel selection, and enabled continuous batching with a 30ms max latency window. Also enabled prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts — that shaved about 15-20% off per-token compute for the 1k cases.

[01:40] Tom Harris: That 30ms batching window, did you try 20ms or 50ms? Curious about latency tail.

[01:44] Maya Singh: We did a sweep: 10/20/30/50ms. 10ms gives slightly better p50 but reduces batching efficiency, tokens/sec drops by ~12%. 50ms improves tokens/sec another 8% but p99 creeps up ~10-12% — so 30ms was the sweet spot for your latency target of <1.5s p99 on 1k seq.

[02:10] Emily Chen: Our SLA target was p99 <1.5s for 1k, so Redwood numbers look promising. Can you share the raw CSV?

[02:16] John Park: Yes we'll send the spreadsheet. Action: John to share.

[02:20] Maya Singh: A quick note on batching: the baseline provider was using a fixed microbatch size and didn't have prefix cache, so their tokens/sec suffered on repeated contexts. Also their kernel selector doesn't pick the f32->int8 path as aggressively for q4x; our runtime picks a better kernel for the attention on 4k sequences which helps the larger seqs.

[02:46] Raj Patel: Did you test with the quantized 3-bit profile we discussed last week? We were worried about quality regressions for clinical text.

[02:52] Maya Singh: We ran quick subjective evals with q3 and q4 and q3 showed a small drop on hallucination for some prompts — not huge but noticeable in edge cases. For compliance-sensitive output we recommend q4 for now; if you want we can run a larger eval set.

[03:10] Sophie Liu: On the infra side — our main concern is network out to Redwood private cluster. If we do an on-prem run we need to ensure the VPC peering doesn't throttle burst throughput. Our infra team saw connection resets at ~1.2Gbps in previous tests. What's the expected throughput for your on-prem package?

[03:30] Maya Singh: For a single GPU running these workloads, you should expect sustained < 600Mbps for typical ops, peak bursts up to ~1.4Gbps depending on the batch size and KV cache hits. If you're seeing resets at 1.2Gbps that's borderline — we'll ask Sophie to share the peering logs and we'll work with infra to tune MTU and parallel streams.

[03:55] Sophie Liu: Will do, I'll send the peering config.

[04:00] Carlos Alvarez: Quick sales/ops question: pricing. With the throughput improvements you saw, roughly what unit cost delta are we estimating vs baseline provider?

[04:09] Maya Singh: Based on current runs, per-token compute cost is about 25% lower once you account for improved tokens/sec and KV hits. I can attach a cost projection. John will include that in the spreadsheet.

[04:22] Emily Chen: That's helpful. The procurement team will want to see that number broken out.

[04:28] Maya Singh: Understood. Also a note about stability: we ran a 90-minute soak with dynamic arrival patterns. Baseline provider started hitting queueing at about 70% load while Redwood kept p99 flat until 85% load due to better autoscale thresholds and smarter fallback routing we configured.

[04:52] Raj Patel: Did the soak include long TTL contexts where KV cache warmed up?

[04:57] Maya Singh: Yes, KV warmed after about 15 min on repeated users. That improved tail latencies for repeat traces, which is relevant since a lot of your traffic is session-based.

[05:10] Tom Harris: Any notable errors or fails during the soak?

[05:13] Maya Singh: We saw a transient OOM when we momentarily bumped batch size for a spike test — fixed by auto-throttling policy. No crashes otherwise. I'll annotate the run where that happened.

[05:25] Emily Chen: On the security front, procurement asked for SOC2 docs and confirmation about KMS/HSM. Are those available?

[05:31] John Park: Yep. We'll share SOC2 and the KMS integration doc. Redwood supports customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated — can confirm HSM options for enterprise. Action: John to share link.

[05:44] Sophie Liu: If we go Private, do we still get the same kernel selection and KV cache behavior? Or does that change when running on-prem?

[05:52] Maya Singh: The runtime is the same; kernel selection is deterministic given the binary and hardware. Some differences can appear on different GPU drivers or slightly different instruction sets, but we've validated the critical kernels on the hardware you're planning to use. We'll run a targeted on-prem benchmark to validate.

[06:08] Raj Patel: Good. For the on-prem tests can you run with our sample workload and the q4 config, and also include the q3 run just for regression checks?

[06:16] Maya Singh: Yep, we'll do q4 primary, q3 regression. We'll also include the exact kernel mapping and a dump of per-op times so you can inspect.

[06:24] Tom Harris: About model fallbacks — if you run out of capacity on dedicated can Redwood automatically route to hosted and what is the latency penalty?

[06:31] Maya Singh: Yes, routing policy can fallback to hosted or to a larger instance pool. Penalty depends on route; region-to-region adds ~120-180ms plus any extra queueing. We can configure graceful degradation policies for you — e.g., degrade to smaller model with same prompt structure or route low-priority requests to hosted.

[06:55] Emily Chen: We want predictable latency for critical flows, so fallback needs to be explicit in SLAs.

[07:00] John Park: Noted. We'll include recommended fallback policies and SLA language for the pilot contract.

[07:06] Maya Singh: Ok back to numbers, here's a sample lines from the CSV:
[07:10] Maya Singh: "1k seq, baseline: p50 210ms, p95 720ms, p99 1800ms, tokens/sec 420"
[07:18] Maya Singh: "1k seq, redwood: p50 170ms, p95 590ms, p99 1200ms, tokens/sec 610"
[07:25] Maya Singh: "4k seq, baseline: p50 780ms, p95 2200ms, p99 3900ms, tokens/sec 300"
[07:33] Maya Singh: "4k seq, redwood: p50 620ms, p95 1680ms, p99 2700ms, tokens/sec 430"

[07:40] Raj Patel: That's a pretty big delta on 4k seq. Are there any quality tradeoffs from the kernel choices?

[07:44] Maya Singh: No quality tradeoffs — kernel choice is about numerical equivalence; quantization and reduced precision would affect quality. Here we used q4 profiles with per-channel scale to keep parity.

[07:58] Sophie Liu: One more infra question — what logging and trace hooks will we get for audits? We need request IDs passed through and token-level cost breakdowns for billing transparency.

[08:10] Carlos Alvarez: We provide per-request trace IDs, token-level costing, and you can opt-in for extended retention for an add-on. We'll include the retention options and log schema in the docs we send.

[08:22] Emily Chen: Good. For next week's run — can we also include a 'no-cache' baseline? Baseline provider didn't use prefix caching so it's good to see the delta with caching off too.

[08:33] Maya Singh: Yes we'll include three variants next time: no-cache, cache-enabled, and cache-enabled + aggressive batching. That'll show the incremental gains.

[08:42] Tom Harris: And please flag the exact commit/hash of the runtime used for reproducibility.

[08:47] Maya Singh: Will do.

[08:50] Emily Chen: Thanks all. Any blockers?

[08:55] Sophie Liu: I'll send peering config and logs by Thursday.

[08:59] Raj Patel: I'll send sample traces and pass/fail metric definitions for our clinical QA.

[09:05] John Park: Great. Quick recap — John will send spreadsheet, SOC2 and KMS docs; Maya will run on-prem tests with q4 primary and q3 regression and attach raw op times; Sophie and Raj will share infra/traces. We'll meet same time next week.

[09:23] Emily Chen: Sounds good thanks everyone.

[09:26] John Park: Thanks — end call.
notes: Customer is largely happy with latency improvements; main open risk is on-prem networking and quantization QA for clinical text
Redwood showed ~25-35% throughput improvement and ~30% better p99 on tested workloads
Next run to include no-cache baseline and on-prem validation
